article_title: Voyager Universal Literacy System®
citation: Voyager Universal Literacy System® — WWC Intervention Report. (2007). What Works Clearinghouse, U.S. Department of Education. https://www.voyagerlearning.com
title: Progress-monitoring and tiered supplemental support structure within a core reading program
description: The program embeds regular assessment into core instruction: it "emphasizes regular assessments, with biweekly reviews for struggling students and quarterly assessments for all students," using a progress monitoring system four times a year. Struggling readers receive supplemental in-school instruction and, if they continue to struggle, may enroll in an 80-hour summer reading intervention program. A home study curriculum with 15-minute parent activities and a take-home library extend the program beyond school.
requirements: A progress monitoring system with an online data management system; reading coaches and ongoing professional development
target_learners: Kindergarten through third-grade students, with additional support for struggling readers
target_learning_goals: Early literacy acquisition and timely identification of struggling readers
examples: Struggling readers are provided with 10–20 minutes of supplemental in-school instruction; each child receives a take-home library to initiate the child's own book collection
key_sources: Voyager Universal Literacy System® — WWC Intervention Report. (2007). What Works Clearinghouse, U.S. Department of Education. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/InterventionReport/538

article_title: Vocabulary enhancement activities and reading for meaning in second language vocabulary acquisition
citation: T. Sima Paribakht and Marjorie Wesche. (1996). Vocabulary enhancement activities and reading for meaning in second language vocabulary acquisition. Second Language Vocabulary Acquisition: A Rationale for Pedagogy, Cambridge University Press. https://doi.org/10.1017/CBO9781139524643.013
title: Vocabulary Knowledge Scale (VKS)
description: The Vocabulary Knowledge Scale is a recently developed instrument for tracking the acquisition of targeted vocabulary words, created by Paribakht and Wesche. In this chapter it is used to measure how L2 students' knowledge of targeted words encountered in reading texts develops across the classroom experiments. The authors describe it as "a recently developed instrument, the Vocabulary Knowledge Scale," with references to Paribakht & Wesche (1993) and Wesche & Paribakht (forthcoming).
requirements: Used to track acquisition of targeted words encountered by L2 students in reading texts, as in the chapter's classroom experiments
target_learners: Second language learners in classroom experiments
examples: The chapter's classroom experiments "track the acquisition of these words using a recently developed instrument, the Vocabulary Knowledge Scale."
key_sources: T. Sima Paribakht and Marjorie Wesche. (1996). Vocabulary enhancement activities and reading for meaning in second language vocabulary acquisition. Second Language Vocabulary Acquisition: A Rationale for Pedagogy, Cambridge University Press. https://doi.org/10.1017/CBO9781139524643.013

article_title: Applying Game Learning Analytics to a Voluntary Video Game: Intrinsic Motivation, Persistence, and Rewards in Learning to Program at an Early Age
citation: M. Zapata-Cáceres and E. Martín-Barroso, "Applying Game Learning Analytics to a Voluntary Video Game: Intrinsic Motivation, Persistence, and Rewards in Learning to Program at an Early Age," in IEEE Access, vol. 9, pp. 123588-123602, 2021, doi: 10.1109/ACCESS.2021.3110475
title: Voluntary video game teaching basic computational concepts to early-age children, grounded in intrinsic motivation
description: A voluntary video game addressing basic computational concepts, deployed for early ages and grounded in intrinsic motivation. The abstract notes that game-based environments often lack "sufficient voluntariness to assess aspects related to intrinsic motivation, such as interests, skills, persistence in solving a problem and behavior in response to rewards", which this design makes measurable. Data were collected via game learning analytics for 15 months, with 4124 users playing more than 28187 games.
requirements: Voluntary play so that interests, skills, persistence, and response to rewards can be observed as motivation-related aspects
target_learners: Children aged 3 to 6 years
target_learning_goals: Basic computational concepts / learning to program as a vehicle for Computational Thinking development
examples: The authors deployed the game and analyzed 15 months of game learning analytics, during which 4124 users played more than 28187 games.
key_sources: M. Zapata-Cáceres and E. Martín-Barroso, "Applying Game Learning Analytics to a Voluntary Video Game: Intrinsic Motivation, Persistence, and Rewards in Learning to Program at an Early Age," in IEEE Access, vol. 9, pp. 123588-123602, 2021, doi: 10.1109/ACCESS.2021.3110475. https://doi.org/10.1109/access.2021.3110475

article_title: Effects of Peer Tutoring With Audio Prompting on Vocabulary Acquisition for Struggling Readers
citation: Mackiewicz, S. M., Wood, C. L., Cooke, N. L., & Mazzotti, V. L. (2011). Effects of Peer Tutoring With Audio Prompting on Vocabulary Acquisition for Struggling Readers. Remedial and Special Education, 32(4), 345–354. https://doi.org/10.1177/0741932510362507
title: VoicePod audio prompting device for naïve peer tutors
description: The VoicePod (Attainment Company Inc., 2006) is "a portable digital recording and playback system that includes multiple, reusable cards." Each card holds a printed text prompt behind a plastic sleeve and an activation strip that plays a recording of up to 10 s when inserted into the pod. In this study eight cards per target word carried the word, definition, example sentences, and fill-in-the-blank items, giving naïve tutors audio models so they could provide correct modeling and feedback. The device was chosen because it was transportable, easily adapted, and cost efficient (about $60 each).
requirements: Tutors must activate the card's recording after each tutee response so feedback can be checked against the recorded model
constraints: Recordings are limited to up to 10 s per card activation
target_learners: fourth-grade struggling readers, including students with high-incidence disabilities
target_learning_goals: vocabulary word meanings and use of words in sentence context
examples: Each tutoring pair received one VoicePod and six sets of eight cards; tutors used the recordings to verify tutee answers during four sessions per week
key_sources: Mackiewicz, S. M., Wood, C. L., Cooke, N. L., & Mazzotti, V. L. (2011). Effects of Peer Tutoring With Audio Prompting on Vocabulary Acquisition for Struggling Readers. Remedial and Special Education, 32(4), 345–354. https://doi.org/10.1177/0741932510362507

article_title: Cardiorespiratory Fitness Is Associated with Selective Attention in Healthy Male High-School Students
citation: Wengaard E, Kristoffersen M, Harris A and Gundersen H (2017) Cardiorespiratory Fitness Is Associated with Selective Attention in Healthy Male High-School Students. Front. Hum. Neurosci. 11:330. https://doi.org/10.3389/fnhum.2017.00330
title: Directly measured maximal oxygen uptake test protocol for assessing cardiorespiratory fitness in adolescents
description: The study assessed cardiorespiratory fitness with an incremental treadmill test to volitional exhaustion, using a metabolic system with a 4.2-L mixing chamber. Oxygen uptake was recorded at 30-s intervals, and VO2max was defined when two of three criteria were satisfied: attaining a VO2-plateau, attaining a HR >90% of age-predicted maximum, and attaining a respiratory exchange ratio >1.1. The average of the two highest consecutive 30-s VO2 values was recorded as individual VO2max.
requirements: 10-min warm-up with gradient of 1.7% on a motorized treadmill
Incremental protocol with treadmill-gradient of 5.3% and start velocity of 8 km/h, speed increased 1 km/h each minute until volitional exhaustion
Full system calibration before testing each group and regular volume calibration with a 3 L syringe
constraints: Participants were excluded if diagnosed with heart disease, asthma or any disease potentially affecting the cardiorespiratory system
Participants were asked not to engage in strenuous physical exercise the day before the physical test
target_learners: healthy male high-school students
examples: Participants demonstrated above average cardiorespiratory fitness (VO2max score of 54.2 ± 4.9 mL·kg−1·min−1) compared to the age-relative norm of the population (46–50 mL·kg−1·min−1)
key_sources: Wengaard E, Kristoffersen M, Harris A and Gundersen H (2017) Cardiorespiratory Fitness Is Associated with Selective Attention in Healthy Male High-School Students. Front. Hum. Neurosci. 11:330. https://doi.org/10.3389/fnhum.2017.00330

article_title: Children’s inference generation: The role of vocabulary and working memory
citation: Currie, N. K., & Cain, K. (2015). Children's inference generation: The role of vocabulary and working memory. Journal of Experimental Child Psychology, 137, 57–75. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jecp.2015.03.005
title: Dual-route account: vocabulary supports inference making through word-meaning knowledge and through boosting maintenance of information in working memory
description: The article proposes that vocabulary knowledge supports children's inference making in two ways. First, "inferences involve word knowledge"; local coherence inferences require mapping between synonyms and category exemplars, and global coherence inferences tap knowledge about interrelations between word meanings. Second, children with richer vocabulary have more accurate and available word representations in long-term memory, which supports accurate maintenance of information in verbal working memory during text integration. The mediation findings are read as evidence for this account.
requirements: Assessment of both breadth and depth of vocabulary, since a single receptive vocabulary measure may not tap deeper knowledge of interrelations between words
constraints: The article notes local and global coherence inferences are not truly categorical distinctions; different inferences draw on text information and background knowledge to differing degrees
target_learners: Children aged 6 to 10 years listening to or reading narrative text
target_learning_goals: Generating local and global coherence inferences during discourse comprehension
key_sources: Currie, N. K., & Cain, K. (2015). Children's inference generation: The role of vocabulary and working memory. Journal of Experimental Child Psychology, 137, 57–75. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jecp.2015.03.005

article_title: ReaderBench: Automated evaluation of collaboration based on cohesion and dialogism
citation: Mihai Dascalu, Stefan Trausan-Matu, Danielle S. Mcnamara, Philippe Dessus. (2015). ReaderBench – Automated Evaluation of Collaboration based on Cohesion and Dialogism. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-015-9226-y
title: Dialogical voice-synergy model of collaboration as transversal analysis of discussion slices
description: The article's second model assesses collaboration "from a dialogical perspective" as the participation of different speakers through their voices. Collaboration is seen as "the intertwining or synergy of voices pertaining to different speakers", enabling "a transversal analysis of subsequent discussion slices". This complements the longitudinal cohesion-graph model by capturing how voices are interwoven across slices of the chat.
requirements: Requires segmentation of the chat into successive discussion slices to which the transversal analysis is applied.
target_learners: Participants in CSCL chat conversations
target_learning_goals: Assessing the intertwining of participants' voices in dialogue
key_sources: Mihai Dascalu, Stefan Trausan-Matu, Danielle S. Mcnamara, Philippe Dessus. (2015). ReaderBench – Automated Evaluation of Collaboration based on Cohesion and Dialogism. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-015-9226-y

article_title: Half a century of Instructional Science: a bibliometric analysis
citation: Betzabe Ruiz-Morales, Víctor G. Alfaro-García, José M. Merigó, Amara Atif, Eleni A. Kyza. (2026). Half a century of Instructional Science: a bibliometric analysis. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09791-6
title: VOS viewer bibliographic mapping of Instructional Science (co-citation, bibliographic coupling, keyword co-occurrence)
description: The study uses VOS viewer software (Van Eck & Waltman, 2010) to graphically map the journal's bibliographic data. It "generates maps based on bibliographic coupling, citation, co-citation, co-authorship, and the co-occurrence of author keywords", applied to the 1,262 articles and reviews retrieved from the WoS Core Collection for 1972–2023. The mapping complements the performance analysis with visual identification of topic clusters and research profiles.
requirements: A bibliographic database export (the study used the WoS Core Collection) and the VOS viewer software to compile and generate the maps
constraints: The analysis is limited to WoS data and its language coverage, and the authors note it is not easy to compare different subfields and variables since they may have different publication and citation characteristics
target_learners: Researchers and bibliometric analysts in the learning sciences
target_learning_goals: Understanding publication, citation and topic trends in a learning-sciences journal over five decades
examples: The article applies the SPAR-4-SLR protocol (Fig. 1) to assemble, arrange and assess 1,262 documents, then maps them via co-citation, bibliographic coupling and keyword co-occurrence
key_sources: Betzabe Ruiz-Morales, Víctor G. Alfaro-García, José M. Merigó, Amara Atif, Eleni A. Kyza. (2026). Half a century of Instructional Science: a bibliometric analysis. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09791-6

article_title: Improving second-grade reading comprehension through a sustained content literacy intervention: A mixed-methods study examining the mediating role of domain-specific vocabulary.
citation: Mosher, D. M., Burkhauser, M. A., & Kim, J. S. (2024). Improving second-grade reading comprehension through a sustained content literacy intervention: A mixed-methods study examining the mediating role of domain-specific vocabulary. Journal of Educational Psychology, 116(4), 550–568. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000868
title: Theory of change: networks of domain-specific vocabulary as the visible components of schemas mediate comprehension transfer
description: The article's theoretical framework holds that schemas are "an abstract knowledge structure" whose visible components are semantically related networks of vocabulary words. Teaching domain-specific words in conceptually related networks helps students build topic and domain schemas, instantiate them during reading via construction-integration processes, and transfer them to related topics. The intervention theory of change links thematic lessons, concept mapping, interactive read alouds, argumentative writing, collaborative research, and word inquiry to vocabulary growth, which in turn supports word-to-text integration on transfer passages.
requirements: Sustained, aligned content literacy instruction across grades so topic schemas accumulate over time
Vocabulary taught in semantic networks rather than in isolation
constraints: Building science and social studies topic knowledge takes time in the early grades; most studies examine only one year
target_learners: early elementary students (Grades 1–2)
examples: The Grade 2 MORE unit on how paleontologists study dinosaurs used concept maps, read alouds, notetaking, word inquiry, and collaborative research across five 9-lesson cycles
key_sources: Mosher, D. M., Burkhauser, M. A., & Kim, J. S. (2024). Improving second-grade reading comprehension through a sustained content literacy intervention: A mixed-methods study examining the mediating role of domain-specific vocabulary. Journal of Educational Psychology, 116(4), 550–568. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000868

article_title: Vocational interest profiles in secondary school: Accounting for multiplicity and exploring associations with future-oriented choices.
citation: Slot, E. M., Bronkhorst, L. H., Akkerman, S. F., & Wubbels, T. (2021). Vocational Interest Profiles in Secondary School: Accounting for Multiplicity and Exploring Associations With Future-Oriented Choices. Journal of Educational Psychology, 113(5), 1059–1071. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000475
title: Multiplicity of vocational interests: profiles as combinations of RIASEC domains rather than single dominant interests
description: This framework treats vocational interests as combinations across the six RIASEC domains (realistic, investigative, artistic, social, enterprising, conventional) rather than assuming one dominant interest per student. The article argues that "vocational interest assessment tools generally do not account for the possibility that students are interested in multiple vocational domains", which can challenge future-oriented decision-making. Latent profile analysis operationalizes this by identifying seven distinct profiles, spanning nondifferentiated (low, neutral, or broad) and differentiated (domain-dominant) structures.
requirements: Assessment of all six RIASEC interest domains so that combinations and profile structures can be identified
constraints: Studied among Dutch secondary school Grade 9 students facing early educational career decisions
target_learners: secondary school students
key_sources: Slot, E. M., Bronkhorst, L. H., Akkerman, S. F., & Wubbels, T. (2021). Vocational Interest Profiles in Secondary School: Accounting for Multiplicity and Exploring Associations With Future-Oriented Choices. Journal of Educational Psychology, 113(5), 1059–1071. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000475

article_title: Nurturing the reading brain: home literacy practices are associated with children’s neural response to printed words through vocabulary skills
citation: Girard, C., Bastelica, T., Léone, J., Epinat-Duclos, J., Longo, L. & Prado, J. (2021). Nurturing the reading brain: home literacy practices are associated with children's neural response to printed words through vocabulary skills. npj Science of Learning 6:34. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00112-9
title: Vocabulary-mediation model of home literacy effects on the reading brain
description: The article tests a hypothesized model in which home literacy experiences scaffold reading via cognitive precursors. As stated, "more frequent home literacy activities may improve children's reading efficiency by fostering vocabulary skills (which are an important foundation for word recognition)", and vocabulary is posited to influence the neural mechanisms supporting word-level reading. The study's behavioral, ROI, and mediation results are interpreted against this model.
requirements: Home literacy practices measured via parental report of informal and formal literacy activity frequency
Children's vocabulary assessed with a standardized measure
constraints: The cross-sectional design does not allow formal testing of causal claims in the model; other models, such as practices increasing in response to children's reading skill, remain compatible with the findings
target_learners: children around age 8 learning to read
examples: Parents of 66 French 8-year-olds reported practice frequency on a six-point scale; mediation analysis in the fMRI subsample tested vocabulary as the mediator between practices and pIFs word adaptation
key_sources: Girard, C., Bastelica, T., Léone, J., Epinat-Duclos, J., Longo, L. & Prado, J. (2021). Nurturing the reading brain: home literacy practices are associated with children's neural response to printed words through vocabulary skills. npj Science of Learning 6:34. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00112-9

article_title: The Power of Voice to Convey Emotion in Multimedia Instructional Messages
citation: Lawson, A. P., & Mayer, R. E. (2022). The Power of Voice to Convey Emotion in Multimedia Instructional Messages. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00282-y
title: When the goal is to convey positive emotion, narrated slides with voice-over can substitute for an embodied onscreen agent
description: This design principle holds that for positive emotional tone, the instructor's recorded voice carries enough affective information that an embodied onscreen agent adds no measurable benefit in emotion recognition. The article states that "when the goal is to convey positive emotion, instructional designers may be able to present narrated slides with voice-over rather than to go to the expense of also adding onscreen embodied agents." It rests on the finding that voice alone matched voice plus agent for happy, content, and bored instructors, and it can lower production cost since many existing videos, such as Khan Academy's, already use disembodied voice.
requirements: A recorded human voice conveying the intended emotional tone in the narrated slideshow
constraints: When the goal is to convey more nuanced or unexpected emotions, such as frustration, the article states "it may be necessary to present both voice and embodiment cues"
The clips studied were all under a minute, so generalization to longer lessons is untested
target_learners: adult online learners in multimedia instructional settings
target_learning_goals: recognizing the positive or negative emotional tone of an instructor in instructional video
examples: Participants in the experiment rated the emotional tone of 16 short clips from a statistics lesson, half with the animated instructor on screen and half with voice-over only
key_sources: Lawson, A. P., & Mayer, R. E. (2022). The Power of Voice to Convey Emotion in Multimedia Instructional Messages. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00282-y

article_title: Basic Life Support Training Methods for Health Science Students: A Systematic Review.
citation: García-Suárez, M., Méndez-Martínez, C., Martínez-Isasi, S., Gómez-Salgado, J., & Fernández-García, D. (2019). Basic Life Support Training Methods for Health Science Students: A Systematic Review. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph16050768
title: Voice advisory mannequin (VAM) with feedback and voice prompts for self-directed CPR training
description: A training mannequin equipped with a feedback system and voice prompts that correct errors during CPR practice, enabling self-directed learning without a continuous instructor presence. The review identifies it as the most effective resource analysed for CPR skill learning among health science students, noting it "allows them to correct their mistakes or undertake knowledge refreshers independently". It appeared in four of the eleven reviewed trials as the intervention device.
requirements: Used as part of practical skills training alongside theoretical content, typically guided by AHA or ERC recommendations
constraints: In one reviewed trial (Isbye et al.), the instructor-led group outperformed VAM self-directed groups immediately, and ventilations were not improved at first
target_learners: nursing students
medicine students
examples: In Kardong-Edgren et al., the mannequin-based (VAM) group obtained the best results in all individual skills except frequency and compressions:ventilations ratio
key_sources: García-Suárez, M., Méndez-Martínez, C., Martínez-Isasi, S., Gómez-Salgado, J., & Fernández-García, D. (2019). Basic Life Support Training Methods for Health Science Students: A Systematic Review. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph16050768

article_title: Vocabulary Enrichment Intervention Programme: Evaluation Report and Executive Summary
citation: Styles, B., Stevens, E., Bradshaw, S., & Clarkson, R. (2014). Vocabulary Enrichment Intervention Programme Evaluation Report and Executive Summary. Education Endowment Foundation. http://www.controlled-trials.com/ISRCTN67513320/
title: Vocabulary Enrichment Full Programme (VEFP): a combined literacy intervention for low-attaining Year 7 pupils
description: The VEFP combines three existing programmes: the Vocabulary Enrichment Intervention Programme (VEIP), a "structured scheme that teaches children new words and encourages them to use these words in speaking and writing"; Sounds-Write, a phonics programme; and Literacy Plus, a Key Stage 3 scheme supporting progress from Level 3 to Level 4 in English. Bolton Local Authority devised the full programme, with VEIP as the core element, and schools were encouraged to build their own scheme of work. Existing class teachers delivered it in place of usual English lessons for approximately 19 teaching weeks, with supervision from an educational psychologist.
requirements: Teachers received training on all three elements and regular supervision and support from an educational psychologist based at Bolton Local Authority
VEIP was required to be the principal component of delivery
constraints: The report states the intervention should be seen as being at the efficacy trial stage of development, tested under developer-led conditions
The evaluation found no evidence of impact on reading attainment
target_learners: Year 7 pupils who had not reached a secure Level 4 in English at the end of Key Stage 2
target_learning_goals: literacy catch-up at the primary-secondary transition
examples: In the trial, delivery varied between schools in lesson duration (50-60 minutes), lessons per week (three to five), and group size (six to 30 at the outset)
key_sources: Styles, B., Stevens, E., Bradshaw, S., & Clarkson, R. (2014). Vocabulary Enrichment Intervention Programme Evaluation Report and Executive Summary. Education Endowment Foundation. http://www.controlled-trials.com/ISRCTN67513320/

article_title: Benefiting from Listening in Vocabulary Development
citation: Berker Bulut, Nuri Karasakaloğlu. (2017). Benefiting from Listening in Vocabulary Development. Journal of Education and Training Studies, Vol. 5, No. 12. https://doi.org/10.11114/jets.v5i12.2688
title: Researcher-developed 50-item Vocabulary Test (KR-20 = .93)
description: A "Vocabulary Test" developed by the researcher to measure fourth-grade students' vocabulary achievement, built from a question pool of 85 items aligned with the Primary Education Turkish Curriculum. After expert review and item analysis (eliminating items with discrimination index below .30 and difficulty outside .10–.90), "the V ocabulary Test consisting of 50 items was prepared". Mean difficulty was .59 and KR-20 was .93.
requirements: Administered as pre-test and post-test to both groups; trial forms were piloted with 226 students from seven different schools
constraints: Designed for fourth-grade vocabulary acquisitions in the Turkish curriculum
target_learners: fourth-grade primary school students
examples: Used as both pre-test and post-test in the semi-experimental study; item analysis results for difficulty (Pj), standard deviation (Sj) and discrimination (rpbi) are printed in Table 3
key_sources: Berker Bulut, Nuri Karasakaloğlu. (2017). Benefiting from Listening in Vocabulary Development. Journal of Education and Training Studies, Vol. 5, No. 12. https://doi.org/10.11114/jets.v5i12.2688

article_title: The Effect of Using Computer-Assisted Language Learning (CALL) on Iranian EFL Learners' Vocabulary Learning: An Experimental Study
citation: Nejati, E., Jahangiri, A. & Salehi, M. R. (2018). The effect of using computer-assisted language learning (CALL) on Iranian EFL learners’ vocabulary learning: An experimental study. Cypriot Journal of Educational Science. 13(2), 351–362. https://www.cjes.eu
title: Vocaboly multimedia software for computer-assisted vocabulary instruction
description: Vocaboly is the multimedia software the study used to teach vocabulary to the experimental groups. It "has several parts such as ‘Study’, ‘Test’ and ‘Game’", including word lists with meaning, difficulty level and phonetic symbol, pronunciation playback, spelling practice with corrective feedback, multiple-choice testing in two modes, and the ‘memory’ and ‘star war’ games. Sessions used prepared source files of ten words each, delivered over eight 15-minute sessions.
requirements: Students needed laptops with the software installed and an introductory familiarisation session to diminish the effect of unfamiliarity with the software.
target_learners: pre-intermediate and intermediate EFL learners (14–18 years old)
target_learning_goals: English vocabulary knowledge including meaning, pronunciation and spelling
examples: Experimental groups loaded a session source file each session, practised word lists, spelling, multiple-choice tests and games, then sat post-tests after eight sessions.
key_sources: Nejati, E., Jahangiri, A. & Salehi, M. R. (2018). The effect of using computer-assisted language learning (CALL) on Iranian EFL learners’ vocabulary learning: An experimental study. Cypriot Journal of Educational Science. 13(2), 351–362. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1183258

article_title: Effects of Two and Three-Dimensional Visual Objects on the Acquisition of Drawing Skills among JSS1 Students in Osun State, Nigeria
citation: Bada Tayo Abass, Bello Isyakka, Ijisakin Yemi Olaolu & Fajuyigbe Michael Olusegun. (2014). Effects of Two and Three-Dimensional Visual Objects on the Acquisition of Drawing Skills among JSS1 Students in Osun State, Nigeria. World Journal of Education, 4(1). https://doi.org/10.5430/wje.v4n1p62
title: Visual Object Achievement Test (VOAT)
description: The Visual Object Achievement Test (VOAT) is the research instrument used in this study to measure JSS1 students' drawing-skill achievement. It was "a fifteen  item objective questions to evaluate the level of mastery of content taught", after which students "were later asked to draw from two-dimensional and three-dimensional visual objects". It was administered as both pretest and post-test across the three groups.
requirements: Administered as pretest before treatment and as post-test after the two-week treatment period to measure mastery of the taught content.
target_learners: Junior Secondary School One (JSS1) students
examples: The first lesson was used for the pretest administration of VOAT to establish prior knowledge before the visual-object treatments began.
key_sources: Bada Tayo Abass, Bello Isyakka, Ijisakin Yemi Olaolu & Fajuyigbe Michael Olusegun. (2014). Effects of Two and Three-Dimensional Visual Objects on the Acquisition of Drawing Skills among JSS1 Students in Osun State, Nigeria. World Journal of Education, 4(1). https://doi.org/10.5430/wje.v4n1p62

article_title: The Impact of Explicit Instruction and Intentional Learning in the Reception of Vocabulary--An Experimental Study
citation: R. Infanta Vincy. (2018). The Impact of Explicit Instruction and Intentional Learning in the Reception of Vocabulary - An Experimental Study. i-manager's Journal on English Language Teaching, Vol. 8 No. 2. https://journals.imanager.com/jelt
title: Vocabulary Knowledge Scale (VKS) self-report instrument for receptive and productive vocabulary development
description: The VKS (Wesche and Paribakht, 1996) is a self-report assessment in line with Dale's (1965) incremental stages of word learning, with five categories ranging from not remembering the word to being able to use it in a sentence. Bruton (2009) called it one of the instruments best known for measuring receptive and productive development of specific targeted words. Because this study focused solely on receptive knowledge, the fifth category was excluded.
requirements: Learners self-analyse their knowledge of each target word across the scale's categories
constraints: The fifth (productive use) category was excluded in this study, which measured only reception
target_learners: fifth-grade second language learners of English
target_learning_goals: self-assessed receptive knowledge of target words
examples: The test was completed in fifteen minutes in Session One, with the researcher reading out words and translating the choices.
key_sources: R. Infanta Vincy. (2018). The Impact of Explicit Instruction and Intentional Learning in the Reception of Vocabulary - An Experimental Study. i-manager's Journal on English Language Teaching, Vol. 8 No. 2. https://journals.imanager.com/jelt

article_title: A Vocabulary-Added Reading Intervention for English Learners At-Risk of Reading Difficulties
citation: Filippini, A. L., Gerber, M. M., & Leafstedt, J. M. (2012). A Vocabulary-Added Reading Intervention for English Learners At-Risk of Reading Difficulties. International Journal of Special Education, 27(3). https://www.internationaljournalofspecialeducation.com
title: Dedicate limited instructional minutes to vocabulary building alongside phonological awareness and decoding in early literacy interventions for at-risk readers
description: The article argues that early interventions focused exclusively on word-level skills can leave students fluent but unable to comprehend, and that vocabulary can be added without sacrificing decoding gains. It "demonstrates initial justification for dedicating limited instructional minutes to vocabulary building in early literacy interventions while still dedicating a small portion of time to phonological awareness and decoding." In the study this meant 70% of supplementary minutes on vocabulary and 30% on PA and decoding within the same total time.
requirements: Supplementary instruction delivered within existing classroom language arts time without increasing total instructional minutes
Trained instructors using a structured, high-response-rate instructional model
constraints: Findings are exploratory with no statistically reliable between-group differences; the authors call for larger samples before efficacy claims
The separation of semantic-relations and morphological-awareness conditions was artificial and could be abandoned for a more cohesive model
target_learners: First-grade English Learners at risk of reading difficulty
Students in high-poverty Title I schools
examples: Vocab+ classrooms taught Tier II words drawn from weekly expository read-alouds while retaining a 30% share of time for PA and decoding, compared with 100% PAD in the treatment-control condition.
key_sources: Filippini, A. L., Gerber, M. M., & Leafstedt, J. M. (2012). A Vocabulary-Added Reading Intervention for English Learners At-Risk of Reading Difficulties. International Journal of Special Education, 27(3). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1001055

article_title: A Vocabulary-Added Reading Intervention for English Learners At-Risk of Reading Difficulties
citation: Filippini, A. L., Gerber, M. M., & Leafstedt, J. M. (2012). A Vocabulary-Added Reading Intervention for English Learners At-Risk of Reading Difficulties. International Journal of Special Education, 27(3). https://www.internationaljournalofspecialeducation.com
title: Vocab+ vocabulary-added intervention (semantic-relations and morphological-awareness variants)
description: A supplementary push-in classroom intervention for first-grade English Learners combining explicit vocabulary instruction with phonological awareness and decoding. Words were Tier II words drawn from weekly expository passage read-alouds, introduced with "synonyms, antonyms, pictures, examples and non-examples, and definitional sentences," and revisited across the eight weeks. The SR variant taught grouping, comparing, and semantic feature analysis of word meanings; the MA variant taught roots, inflectional and derivational suffixes, and word formation through activities such as a cubes game.
requirements: Small-group instruction by trained researchers within regularly scheduled language arts time
An average of 15 minutes per day, four days a week, for eight weeks
Weekly expository passage read-aloud shared across conditions
constraints: Evaluated only with first-grade, primarily Spanish-speaking English Learners in one Title I school
Vocabulary outcomes were measured with an experimental true/false sentence test of taught words
target_learners: First-grade English Learners at risk of reading difficulty
examples: In the grab bag activity, instructors tracked pulled words to ensure review words as well as novel words were discussed; in the cubes game students combined root-word and suffix cubes to form words.
key_sources: Filippini, A. L., Gerber, M. M., & Leafstedt, J. M. (2012). A Vocabulary-Added Reading Intervention for English Learners At-Risk of Reading Difficulties. International Journal of Special Education, 27(3). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1001055

article_title: Mind Map Technique in Physical Education: Development of Cognitive and Psychomotor Skills
citation: Temiz, C. N., & Sivrikaya, A. H. (2023). Mind map technique in physical education: Development of cognitive and psychomotor skills. Kuramsal Eğitimbilim Dergisi [Journal of Theoretical Educational Science], 16(1), 20-40. http://doi.org/10.30831/akukeg.1175006
title: Volleyball Knowledge Test and Volleyball Skill Test instruments
description: The study used two instruments: a Volleyball Knowledge Test for the cognitive domain, developed from MoNE (2018) curriculum outcomes and refined from a 24-question draft to a final test after expert review and psychometric evaluation, and a Volleyball Skill Test observation form covering overhand pass, bump pass, and underhand serve. The article reports "The KR-20 reliability coefficient o f the test was determined to be .74" for the final knowledge test, which it describes as having a reliability level applicable to the study. The skill form is a 5-point Likert-type scale with predetermined score categories from 1-9 to 37-45.
requirements: Expert review by a commission of curriculum development, measurement and evaluation, PE, and Turkish language specialists
Psychometric evaluation including factor load analyses before use
constraints: Developed specifically for the volleyball unit outcomes specified by the MoNE (2018) primary education curriculum
target_learners: 6th-grade secondary school students
target_learning_goals: Overhand pass, bump pass, and underhand serve skill levels
examples: Administered as pretests before the 9-week intervention and repeated as posttests to both groups
key_sources: Temiz, C. N., & Sivrikaya, A. H. (2023). Mind map technique in physical education: Development of cognitive and psychomotor skills. Kuramsal Eğitimbilim Dergisi [Journal of Theoretical Educational Science], 16(1), 20-40. http://doi.org/10.30831/akukeg.1175006

article_title: Efficacy of a Virtual Teaching Assistant in an Open Laboratory Environment for Electric Circuits
citation: Saleheen, F., Wang, Z., Picone, J., Butz, B. P., and Won, C.-H. (2018). Efficacy of a Virtual Teaching Assistant in an Open Laboratory Environment for Electric Circuits. Advances in Engineering Education. http://www.temple.edu/csnap/volta.html
title: VOLTA: a web-based virtual teaching assistant for an open electric circuits laboratory
description: VOLTA is a web-based application hosted on a cloud-based server that provides laboratory instructions, equipment usage videos, circuit simulation assistance, and hardware implementation diagnostics for students using a portable Digilent EE board. The article states it "supports on-demand learning and provides immediate feedback on lab exercises and quizzes". Its software consists of four modules (Instructor, Student, Help, and Circuit Comparator and tracer) and one database, implemented in Python and Django, with an administration panel for instructors to manage lab content.
requirements: A portable hardware platform (the Digilent EE board with WaveForms software) and web hosting via a cloud-based server
A certain amount of laboratory material development is needed when adapting it to new labs, though the general structure can be reused
constraints: Developed and evaluated for a second-semester undergraduate electric circuits course at one institution
target_learners: undergraduate engineering students in an entry-level electric circuits laboratory
target_learning_goals: electric circuits laboratory skills, including simulation, hardware implementation, and debugging
examples: Students performed lab experiments anywhere at their convenience using the EE module provided free of charge, with 20 instructional videos also available via a YouTube channel 'Temple Volta'
key_sources: Saleheen, F., Wang, Z., Picone, J., Butz, B. P., and Won, C.-H. (2018). Efficacy of a Virtual Teaching Assistant in an Open Laboratory Environment for Electric Circuits. Advances in Engineering Education. http://www.temple.edu/csnap/volta.html

article_title: Effects of Hierarchy Vocabulary Exercises on English Vocabulary Acquisition
citation: Lin, Ching-Ying & Hsu, Wei Shu. (2013). Effects of Hierarchy Vocabulary Exercises on English Vocabulary Acquisition. English Language Teaching, 6(9). http://dx.doi.org/10.5539/elt.v6n9p110
title: Wesche and Paribakht's five-category hierarchy of vocabulary exercise types
description: The article describes a hierarchy of vocabulary exercise types developed by Wesche and Paribakht (1994), comprising "five categories of mental processing which are required to complete various vocabulary exercises": selective attention, recognition, manipulation, interpretation and production. The categories are "hierarchical and are classified according to the learning activities required", moving learners from noticing a target word list, to matching words with definitions, constructing words with stems and affixes, guessing meaning in context, and finally producing the word in answers. The study used exercises built on this hierarchy as its experimental treatment.
requirements: Exercises must draw learners' attention and provide the mental processes required to expand vocabulary, which the article says are indispensable for promoting vocabulary learning
constraints: The article notes extensive reading without vocabulary enhancement exercises was claimed by Wesche and Paribakht to be insufficient for vocabulary retention and gains
target_learners: EFL elementary school students
target_learning_goals: Vocabulary acquisition and retention of target words
examples: The experimental treatment engaged learners through the five mental operations, which the article says processed vocabulary knowledge from a simple stage to a complicated stage, helping learners notice, discern, construct, contextualize, and generate target words stage by stage.
key_sources: Lin, Ching-Ying & Hsu, Wei Shu. (2013). Effects of Hierarchy Vocabulary Exercises on English Vocabulary Acquisition. English Language Teaching, 6(9). http://dx.doi.org/10.5539/elt.v6n9p110

article_title: The Effect of Vocabulary Self-Selection Strategy and Input Enhancement Strategy on the Vocabulary Knowledge of Iranian EFL Learners
citation: Golfam Masoudi. (2017). The Effect of Vocabulary Self-Selection Strategy and Input Enhancement Strategy on the Vocabulary Knowledge of Iranian EFL Learners. English Language Teaching, 10(8). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v10n8p32
title: Vocabulary Self-Selection strategy as an autonomy-building, student-generated word-selection approach
description: Vocabulary Self-Selection (Haggard) is an interactive-learning instructional strategy in which students choose the words they want to learn from their own reading, guess meanings from context in collaborative groups, negotiate definitions with the teacher, and record words on index cards. The article describes it as "based on the self-selection of words during reading", using student-generated rather than preselected word lists, and states it "makes students independent over time". In the study it was implemented in groups of four over 24 sessions with a board vocabulary graph and card games.
requirements: Students read texts and self-select words they believe should be learnt
Group discussion and negotiation of word meanings with teacher facilitation
Recording selected words, sentences and guessed meanings on a vocabulary graph and index cards
constraints: The study applied it with pre-intermediate Iranian EFL learners aged 14-16 in groups of four
target_learners: pre-intermediate Iranian EFL learners aged 14-16
examples: Groups of four learners selected five words per session, presented two to the class on the board vocabulary graph, and played an index-card definition game every three sessions
key_sources: Golfam Masoudi. (2017). The Effect of Vocabulary Self-Selection Strategy and Input Enhancement Strategy on the Vocabulary Knowledge of Iranian EFL Learners. English Language Teaching, 10(8). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v10n8p32

article_title: Teaching Semantic Prosody of English Verbs through the DDL Approach and Its Effect on Learners' Vocabulary Choice Appropriateness in a Persian EFL Context
citation: Mansoory, N. & Jafarpour, M. (2014). Teaching Semantic Prosody of English Verbs through the DDL Approach and its Effect on Learners' Vocabulary Choice Appropriateness in a Persian EFL Context. Advances in Language and Literary Studies, 5(2). https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.5n.2p.149
title: Vocabulary Choice Appropriateness Test: a 30-item three-choice near-synonym instrument with KR-21 reliability of 0.86
description: The study's measurement instrument is a 30-item multiple-choice test with three answer choices per item, built on the assumption that a word's prosodic behavior is positive, neutral, or negative. Each item presents a sentence gap, the original word used, and a near-synonym set; the original word is the keyed answer. The test was piloted with 12 similar male EFL learners over 6 weeks, some items were deleted or changed, and "the reliability estimate for vocabulary choice appropriateness test was 0.86". Validity was checked by five native-speaker judges whose agreement was about 85%.
requirements: Items drawn from corpora used in the study and from researcher-determined or teacher-determined SP cases
Native-speaker judgment to validate keyed answers
constraints: Three-choice items made the test quite easier than four-choice alternatives would have been
The test measured receptive mode only
target_learners: Persian EFL learners at intermediate level
target_learning_goals: Measuring appropriate vocabulary choice based on semantic prosody
examples: Sample item: 'The constantly threatening nuclear war will ---------' with near-synonym set {start, develop, break out}
key_sources: Mansoory, N. & Jafarpour, M. (2014). Teaching Semantic Prosody of English Verbs through the DDL Approach and its Effect on Learners' Vocabulary Choice Appropriateness in a Persian EFL Context. Advances in Language and Literary Studies, 5(2). https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.5n.2p.149

article_title: The Impact of Vodcast Utilisation upon Student Learning of Physiology by First Year Graduate to Entry Medicine Students
citation: Rae, M. G., & McCarthy, M. (2017). The impact of vodcast utilisation upon student learning of Physiology by first year graduate to entry medicine students. Journal of the Scholarship of Teaching and Learning, 17(2), 1-23. https://doi.org/10.14434/josotl.v17i2.21125
title: Providing full-length vodcasts of lecture material in advance of lectures can improve exam performance in accelerated professional programmes.
description: The article argues that making full-length vodcasts of lecture material available to students before lectures enables a 'first pass' exposure that allows deeper cognitive processing during face-to-face time. The authors found that vodcast access was associated with significantly higher CA and EOY exam scores. They recommend this approach particularly for accelerated professional courses like GEM where study demands are high.
requirements: Vodcasts must be made available at least two weeks before the relevant lecture
Students must have access to a virtual learning environment for distribution
constraints: Only 15% of students previewed all vodcasts, so the improvement cannot be attributed solely to previewing
The study was conducted in a single school with a limited number of students on one module component
target_learners: first-year graduate entry medicine students
examples: 73 GEM 1 students were given access to nine full-length vodcasts (mean 47.3±1.9 minutes) via Blackboard at least two weeks before each lecture
key_sources: Rae, M. G., & McCarthy, M. (2017). The impact of vodcast utilisation upon student learning of Physiology by first year graduate to entry medicine students. Journal of the Scholarship of Teaching and Learning, 17(2), 1-23. https://doi.org/10.14434/josotl.v17i2.21125

article_title: Academic motivation-achievement cycle and the behavioural pathways: A short-timeframe experiment with manipulated perceived achievement.
citation: Vu, T., Meeter, M., Hofman, A., Jansen, B., Magis‐Weinberg, L., van Triest, E., & van Atteveldt, N. (2025). Academic motivation–achievement cycle and the behavioural pathways: A short‐timeframe experiment with manipulated perceived achievement. British Journal of Educational Psychology, 95, 683–722. https://doi.org/10.1111/bjep.12731
title: One-hour online vocabulary-learning paradigm with manipulated peer-rank feedback and objective effort measures
description: A computerised English vocabulary-learning task in which participants selected Dutch translations for words they reported not knowing, in blocks of trials with feedback after each block. Feedback contained the actual score plus a manipulated rank among fake participants, first above and then below average. Effort was measured objectively: "The amount of time that participants pressed the mouse button constituted our measure of quantity of effort" and the choice between viewing only the meaning or meaning plus an example sentence was "our measure of quality of effort". Intrinsic motivation was rated on a visual analogue scale after every block.
requirements: Participants must supply a pool of self-reported unknown words (250 per participant drawn from a 1305-word GRE pool) so items are individually novel
A manipulation check at the end to exclude participants who did not believe the rank feedback
constraints: The experiment was conducted online due to COVID-19 restrictions, requiring a computer, mouse and keyboard
Trial durations were bounded between 7 and 12 seconds to limit between-participant differences in trial counts
target_learners: non-native English-speaking undergraduate students
examples: The final sample consisted of 309 participants after excluding 45 who failed the manipulation check or missed time points

Block timing varied across participants (four/four, three/five, or five/three above/below-average blocks) so the setback occurred at different moments, allowing the authors to rule out fatigue as the cause of motivation and effort drops
key_sources: Vu, T., Meeter, M., Hofman, A., Jansen, B., Magis‐Weinberg, L., van Triest, E., & van Atteveldt, N. (2025). Academic motivation–achievement cycle and the behavioural pathways: A short‐timeframe experiment with manipulated perceived achievement. British Journal of Educational Psychology, 95, 683–722. https://doi.org/10.1111/bjep.12731

article_title: Comparison of the adequacies of the OSCE and vOSCE to assess the competencies required under Brazilian medical curriculum guidelines: a multicenter study.
citation: Sampaio Carvalho H, Barros Melo M do C, Kakehasi FM, Menezes Ferri Liu P, Gontijo Minafra Silveira Santos F, de Melo Martins RL, Vale de Castro Monteiro M, Chaves Campos ME, Esteves RZ, Belloni Torsani M, Lopes Calvo T I de F, Inca Atahualpa Urdiales A, De Marco Novellino AM, Viana Zuza DR, Ferreira Moura H, de Vilhena Toledo MA, Machado Saldanha CR, Pedrosa Ribeiro Alves Oliveira A, Zen Tempski P, de Souza Santos I, de Arruda Martins M. (2025). Comparison of the adequacies of the OSCE and vOSCE to assess the competencies required under Brazilian medical curriculum guidelines: a multicenter study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-06631-4
title: Use the vOSCE as a complement to other assessment methodologies, not as the sole means of assessing competencies
description: The article states: "the vOSCE should not be applied as the sole means of assessing competencies in health management. Rather, it should be used as a tool that complements other methodologies." This principle follows from the panel's finding that some competencies (e.g., subjective management skills, physical examinations) exceed what a virtual examination can capture, while the vOSCE remains effective for specific skills such as leadership, decision-making, and communication. It guides institutions integrating vOSCE into assessment programs.
requirements: Complementary methodologies must exist alongside the vOSCE for competencies it cannot reach
constraints: Stated for the health management domain; the article separately identifies physical-examination items as limited under both methods
target_learners: undergraduate medical students and medical residents
target_learning_goals: competency-based assessment of knowledge, skills, and attitudes under the Brazilian DCNs
examples: The panel recommended that broad competencies be embedded in station items for other knowledge domains and that public-health evaluations be conducted in a group work format

(2025). Comparison of the adequacies of the OSCE and vOSCE to assess the competencies required under Brazilian medical curriculum guidelines: a multicenter study. article_title: The Impact of Implementing the Vortex Approach on Airway Management Performance in Stressed Medical Students: A Randomized Controlled Simulation Study.
citation: Starosolski Michał, Kapłan Cezary, Kalemba Alicja, Majewska Karolina. (2023). The Impact of Implementing the Vortex Approach on Airway Management Performance in Stressed Medical Students: A Randomized Controlled Simulation Study. Medical Science Monitor. https://doi.org/10.12659/MSM.940372
title: Introduce simple, flexibly structured decision-support algorithms such as the Vortex Approach early in medical training to reduce cognitive overload during crisis airway management
description: The article recommends integrating the Vortex Approach into the medical curriculum because even a brief exposure improves performance under stress. The Vortex Approach is a decision-support scheme that replaces linear algorithmic steps with the recipient's freedom to move among three upper airway lifelines, described as a tool "to be used in real time by teams of potentially highly stressed individuals". The authors state it should "therefore be included in the learning plan".
requirements: Algorithms introduced should be easy to understand even for an inexperienced audience and easy to recreate in situations of strong cognitive overload
constraints: Based on this work, the authors can only surmise that the form of the algorithm is relevant only in crisis conditions of a difficult airway
target_learners: Medical students in their 4th to 6th year with at least 1 year of clinical classes completed
target_learning_goals: Airway management in emergencies, including ventilation and supraglottic device insertion when intubation fails
examples: After a 10-minute strictly theoretical lecture on the Vortex Approach without practice, the Vortex group performed better airway management in a 7-minute simulated difficult-airway scenario than randomly assigned controls
key_sources: Starosolski Michał, Kapłan Cezary, Kalemba Alicja, Majewska Karolina. (2023). The Impact of Implementing the Vortex Approach on Airway Management Performance in Stressed Medical Students: A Randomized Controlled Simulation Study. Medical Science Monitor. https://doi.org/10.12659/MSM.940372
